tldr: The US added Nvidia customer Megaspeed and six affiliates to the Entity List, including Alibaba's Singapore compute unit Apex, which reportedly prepaid ~$4.2B for Southeast Asian compute; Alibaba calls the listing erroneous and vows legal action.

OpenAI and Cisco open-sourced Shirudo, where agents write signed, operator-approved eBPF 'shields' that block exploits on unpatched Linux, while Anthropic's Claude Ship lets three agents review, fix and approve GitHub PRs. Dell's AI backlog hit a record $132.3B on $54.9B quarterly revenue (+103%), and it lifted its FY27 guide to $202B.

In China, ByteDance opened the beta of Xiaodou, a standalone Doubao personal agent with paid tiers up to ¥500/month, and Baidu open-sourced the 280B-parameter ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview. Huang's return lifted the Taiex a record 8.99%, but Nvidia gave back 5.9% in New York and Anthropic closed below its $83 IPO price.

items.title: US adds Megaspeed and six affiliates, including Alibaba's Singapore unit Apex, to the Entity List; Alibaba vows to fight
items.original_title: 阿里巴巴回应子公司被列入美实体清单：将通过一切法律途径维护公司权益
items.summary: The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security added Nvidia customer Megaspeed International and six related companies in Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand to the Entity List, citing a significant risk that they are or will become involved in diverting advanced computing chips to unauthorised end users. The seven include MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International, Speedmatrix, Swiftdata, Megaspeed (Thailand) and Apex Enterprise Solutions, which Reuters and Bloomberg identify as Alibaba's Singapore compute-procurement subsidiary. US suppliers now need a licence to ship them any items subject to US export rules. Alibaba called the listing 'erroneous', said Apex has never diverted restricted chips, and said it would pursue 'all legal avenues'; Megaspeed denies wrongdoing.
items.why_it_matters: This is the first concrete enforcement action in the Nvidia/Megaspeed affair, and the first time an Alibaba entity has been hit by a US chip-diversion listing. Apex reportedly prepaid about $4.2B to Megaspeed and partners for Southeast Asian compute, so the listing raises the risk for Chinese labs renting US chips abroad.

items.title: OpenAI and Cisco open-source Shirudo, letting AI agents write eBPF shields for unpatched Linux systems
items.summary: OpenAI and Cisco released Shirudo, an open-source Linux runtime in which agents write small temporary eBPF programs ('shields'). Each shield blocks the specific behaviour a vulnerability depends on, so the system needs no reboot while the full patch is tested and rolled out. An operator must approve each shield, and shields are cryptographically signed. In a demo, Codex generated a shield that blocked 'Java4Shell' exploitation on a running Elasticsearch instance. Shirudo builds on Isovalent's Tetragon, is BSD-2-Clause licensed (BPF programs dual BSD/GPL), and needs Shirudo's kernel patches plus TPM 2.0 in production.
items.why_it_matters: This is a frontier lab shipping defensive agent tooling at kernel level, aimed at the patch gap that AI-accelerated exploitation is widening. It also gives Cisco's Isovalent stack a role in agentic security operations.

items.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, agents that review, fix and approve GitHub pull requests
items.summary: Anthropic launched Claude Ship on Nov 23, a beta for Claude Team and Enterprise organisations on GitHub. It bundles three agents: Code Review (already generally available), plus PR Steward and Claude Approvals, both in beta. Claude Approvals follows a policy file each team writes in its repo, and Anthropic suggests starting it in observe-only mode. Developers start it with a /ship command in Claude Code and the desktop app. It is billed by tokens, separately from plan usage, and is unavailable to Zero Data Retention, HIPAA or customer-managed-key organisations.
items.why_it_matters: Letting an agent approve merges, not just comment on them, takes the last human gate in the coding pipeline and makes it policy-driven. That raises the stakes for code-review rivals such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Cognition. Anthropic has published no benchmark and warns it may miss bugs and vulnerabilities.

items.title: ShellBench: best AI agent completes 62.5% of everyday tasks drawn from 10M+ real agent interactions
items.summary: The OpenClaw Foundation, with Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat and UC Berkeley, released ShellBench. It is a benchmark of 100 everyday tasks drawn from more than 10 million anonymised real-world agent interactions, run across five harnesses: Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw and Pi. The top result was GPT-6 Astra at 62.5% ($1.01 per run), with GPT-6.1 Sol at 61.4% for $0.17. Across all models, 15.7% of attempts broke at least one safety requirement. Technical takeaway: with the harness fixed, the median spread between models was 45.7 points; with the model fixed, swapping harnesses gave a median spread of only 6.2 points.
items.why_it_matters: It adds data from real usage to the 'agents aren't ready' debate: frontier agents still fail about 4 in 10 delegated tasks. It also shows that model choice dominates harness choice, which matters for the many agent-harness startups.

items.title: Prosecutors say ex-OpenAI engineer Alfozan likely captured trade secrets on a hidden bug and fight his release
items.summary: In a detention filing, US prosecutors say former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan likely recorded trade secrets with a device hidden behind a TV in an OpenAI conference room. Investigators say they found hundreds of audio files on his personal computer, including dozens of OpenAI meeting recordings from September 2026 and more than 160 hours of audio in total. Prosecutors also cite a photo of a confidential 'strategic partnership' document on his phone and regular contact with people tied to the Saudi government, and say he used OpenAI's Codex to improve the device. Alfozan, who denies spying for Saudi Arabia, is seeking release on a $1M bond, which prosecutors oppose as a flight risk.
items.why_it_matters: This is the most detailed public account yet of insider espionage at a frontier lab, ahead of the Jan 20 trial, and adds pressure on AI labs' physical and insider security controls.

items.summary: Anthropic put zero data retention with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) into public beta for eligible Claude Platform organisations. learn.title: Split an agent benchmark's variance into model, harness and noise
learn.why_today: ShellBench reports a median 45.7-point spread between models with the harness fixed, against only 6.2 points between harnesses with the model fixed, across 100 everyday tasks.
learn.explanation: Treat a models x harnesses score grid as a two-way layout: score = grand mean + model effect + harness effect + interaction/noise. Sums of squares of the row and column means tell you what share of the variation each factor explains, which is more robust than max-min spreads. Spreads are biased upward by noise: with 100 binary tasks a single run at 60% has a standard error of about 4.9 points, so a max-min across five harnesses can show 10+ points even when the true harness effect is small. Before claiming a harness 'matters', compare its effect with the binomial noise floor, rerun with seeds, or use paired tests on the same tasks. The snippet uses synthetic scores, not ShellBench data.
learn.math: SS_{model} = H\sum_m (\bar y_{m\cdot}-\bar y)^2,\quad SS_{harness} = M\sum_h (\bar y_{\cdot h}-\bar y)^2,\quad SE = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}
learn.python:
# Two-way decomposition of agent-benchmark scores: model effect vs harness effect.
# Synthetic, illustrative scores only (not ShellBench data).
import random, statistics as st
random.seed(0)
models = {f"M{i}": random.uniform(20, 65) for i in range(8)}      # true model skill
harness = {h: random.gauss(0, 3) for h in "ABCDE"}                  # small harness offsets
n_tasks = 100
score = {}
for m, mu in models.items():
    for h, off in harness.items():
        p = min(max((mu + off) / 100, 0), 1)
        score[m, h] = 100 * sum(random.random() < p for _ in range(n_tasks)) / n_tasks
grand = st.mean(score.values())
m_eff = {m: st.mean(score[m, h] for h in harness) - grand for m in models}
h_eff = {h: st.mean(score[m, h] for m in models) - grand for h in harness}
ss_m = len(harness) * sum(v * v for v in m_eff.values())
ss_h = len(models) * sum(v * v for v in h_eff.values())
ss_tot = sum((v - grand) ** 2 for v in score.values())
print(f"share of variance: model {ss_m/ss_tot:.0%}, harness {ss_h/ss_tot:.0%}, "
      f"interaction+noise {1-(ss_m+ss_h)/ss_tot:.0%}")
spread_m = st.median(max(score[m, h] for m in models) - min(score[m, h] for m in models) for h in harness)
spread_h = st.median(max(score[m, h] for h in harness) - min(score[m, h] for h in harness) for m in models)
print(f"median spread across models (harness fixed): {spread_m:.1f} pts")
print(f"median spread across harnesses (model fixed): {spread_h:.1f} pts")
# Binomial noise floor: one run on 100 tasks at p=0.6 has SE ~ 4.9 pts
print(f"binomial SE at p=0.6, n={n_tasks}: {100*(0.6*0.4/n_tasks)**0.5:.1f} pts")

learn.title: Price an MoE: memory follows total parameters, decode speed follows active ones
learn.why_today: Baidu's open ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is reported as a mixture-of-experts with 280B total and 14B active parameters per token.
learn.explanation: In a mixture-of-experts model a router sends each token to a few experts, so per-token compute is about 2 FLOPs per active weight, while all experts must still sit in accelerator memory. A 280B/14B MoE therefore needs the memory footprint of a 280B dense model but has the per-token FLOPs of a 14B one. At small batch sizes decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, and the ceiling is roughly bandwidth divided by bytes of active weights read per token, which is why MoEs decode fast. The idea breaks at large batches, where different tokens hit different experts and the whole weight set gets read anyway, and under expert-parallel sharding, where all-to-all communication and load imbalance between experts dominate. The bandwidth and HBM figures in the snippet are illustrative.
learn.python:
# MoE serving arithmetic: memory scales with TOTAL params, per-token compute with ACTIVE.
# 280B total / 14B active matches the reported ERNIE 5.5 Flash headline figures;
# the dense comparison and bandwidth numbers are illustrative.
def serve(total_b, active_b, bytes_per_w=1.0, hbm_gb=141, bw_tbs=4.8):
    weights_gb = total_b * bytes_per_w                # FP8 weights ~1 byte each
    gpus = -(-weights_gb // (hbm_gb * 0.8))           # leave 20% HBM for KV cache
    flops_tok = 2 * active_b * 1e9                    # ~2 FLOPs per active weight
    # Decode at batch 1 is bandwidth-bound: read the active weights once per token
    tok_s = bw_tbs * 1e12 / (active_b * 1e9 * bytes_per_w)
    return weights_gb, int(gpus), flops_tok, tok_s

for name, tot, act in [("MoE 280B/14B", 280, 14), ("dense 70B", 70, 70), ("dense 280B", 280, 280)]:
    w, g, f, t = serve(tot, act)
    print(f"{name:13s} weights={w:5.0f} GB  GPUs(141GB)={g}  "
          f"GFLOPs/token={f/1e9:5.0f}  batch-1 decode ceiling~{t:5.0f} tok/s per GPU-bandwidth")
